claim: SynGAP is a Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that is a major constituent of postsynaptic densities (PSDs) from mammalian forebrain.
source: SynGAP is a Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that is a major constituent of postsynaptic densities (PSDs) from mammalian forebrain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The α1 isoform of synGAP binds to all three PDZ (PSD-95, Discs-large, ZO-1) domains of PSD-95.
source: Its α1 isoform binds to all three PDZ (PSD-95, Discs-large, ZO-1) domains of PSD-95, the principal PSD scaffold
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3A.

claim: SynGAP-α1 can occupy as many as 15% of the PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: Its α1 isoform binds to all three PDZ (PSD-95, Discs-large, ZO-1) domains of PSD-95, the principal PSD scaffold, and can occupy as many as 15% of these PDZ domains.
evidence: This is calculated based on the relative abundance of synGAP-α1 and PSD-95 in the PSD as described in the Introduction.

claim: Phosphorylation by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) decreases synGAP-α1's affinity for the PDZ domains by several fold.
source: We show that phosphorylation by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) and Polo-like kinase-2 (PLK2) decreases its affinity for the PDZ domains by several fold
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figures 3A, 3D, 7A and Table 1, showing approximately 10-fold reduction in affinity.

claim: Phosphorylation by Polo-like kinase-2 (PLK2) decreases synGAP-α1's affinity for the PDZ domains by several fold.
source: We show that phosphorylation by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) and Polo-like kinase-2 (PLK2) decreases its affinity for the PDZ domains by several fold
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3E, showing approximately 40% reduction in binding.

claim: Three critical postsynaptic signaling proteins that bind to the PDZ domains of PSD-95 are present in higher concentration in PSDs isolated from mice with a heterozygous deletion of synGAP.
source: Finally, we show that three critical postsynaptic signaling proteins that bind to the PDZ domains of PSD-95 are present in higher concentration in PSDs isolated from mice with a heterozygous deletion of synGAP.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11, showing increased TARPs, LRRTM2, and neuroligin-2 in Syngap+/- mice.

claim: AMPARs become immobilized at the postsynaptic membrane by a three stage process involving insertion of receptors into the perisynaptic membrane, diffusion into the synapse and 'trapping' within the structure of the postsynaptic density (PSD).
source: Numerous experiments have shown that AMPARs become immobilized at the postsynaptic membrane by a three stage process involving insertion of receptors into the perisynaptic membrane, diffusion into the synapse and 'trapping' within the structure of the postsynaptic density (PSD; Opazo and Choquet, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Opazo and Choquet, 2011.

claim: The sites at which AMPARs are trapped have been referred to as 'slots'.
source: The sites at which the receptors are trapped have been referred to as 'slots,' (Shi et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shi et al., 2001.

claim: AMPAR trapping slots are believed to consist principally of PDZ domains on PSD-95.
source: The sites at which the receptors are trapped have been referred to as 'slots,' (Shi et al., 2001) and they are believed to consist principally of PDZ domains on PSD-95 (Opazo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Opazo et al., 2012.

claim: Phosphorylation by CaMKII of TARPs increases their affinity for PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: Phosphorylation by CaMKII of TARPs (Transmembrane AMPAR Regulatory Proteins; Bredt and Nicoll, 2003) increases their affinity for PDZ domains of PSD-95 suggesting that the phosphorylation may promote trapping of new AMPARs in the PSD (Tomita et al., 2005; Opazo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomita et al., 2005 and Opazo et al., 2010.

claim: The PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for several synaptic regulatory proteins including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs).
source: Indeed the PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for several synaptic regulatory proteins (Figures 1 and 2B); including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs; Kornau et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kornau et al., 1995 and illustrated in Figures 1 and 2B.

claim: The PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for neuroligins.
source: Indeed the PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for several synaptic regulatory proteins (Figures 1 and 2B); including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs; Kornau et al., 1995), as well as neuroligins (Varoqueaux et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Varoqueaux et al., 2006 and illustrated in Figures 1 and 2B.

claim: The PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for LRRTMs (Leucine Rich Repeat TransMembrane proteins).
source: Indeed the PDZ domains of PSD-95 act as docking sites for several synaptic regulatory proteins (Figures 1 and 2B); including NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs; Kornau et al., 1995), as well as neuroligins (Varoqueaux et al., 2006) and LRRTMs (Leucine Rich Repeat TransMembrane proteins; Linhoff et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Linhoff et al., 2009 and illustrated in Figures 1 and 2B.

claim: Neuroligins and LRRTMs nucleate new synapse formation.
source: as well as neuroligins (Varoqueaux et al., 2006) and LRRTMs (Leucine Rich Repeat TransMembrane proteins; Linhoff et al., 2009), which nucleate new synapse formation
evidence: This is supported by citations to Varoqueaux et al., 2006 and Linhoff et al., 2009.

claim: Neuroligins and LRRTMs contribute to clustering of AMPARs.
source: as well as neuroligins (Varoqueaux et al., 2006) and LRRTMs (Leucine Rich Repeat TransMembrane proteins; Linhoff et al., 2009), which nucleate new synapse formation and contribute to clustering of AMPARs (Siddiqui et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Siddiqui et al., 2010.

claim: AMPARs, NMDARs, TARPs, LRRTMs, and neuroligins comprise the most highly enriched transmembrane proteins precipitated together with PSD-95 from the PSD fraction of mouse forebrain.
source: AMPARs, NMDARs, TARPs, LRRTMs, and neuroligins comprise the most highly enriched transmembrane proteins precipitated together with PSD-95 from the PSD fraction of mouse forebrain (Dosemeci et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dosemeci et al., 2007.

claim: SynGAP-α1 contains a PDZ-domain ligand.
source: One prominent alternatively spliced isoform, synGAP-α1 (Li et al., 2001) contains a PDZ-domain ligand and binds to all three of the PDZ domains of PSD-95 (Kim et al., 1998; Figures 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2001 and Kim et al., 1998, and illustrated in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: SynGAP-α1 binds to all three of the PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: One prominent alternatively spliced isoform, synGAP-α1 (Li et al., 2001) contains a PDZ-domain ligand and binds to all three of the PDZ domains of PSD-95 (Kim et al., 1998; Figures 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 1998 and demonstrated in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Phosphorylation of synGAP-α1 on several sites in the regulatory region by at least two protein kinases reduces the affinity of synGAP-α1's PDZ-ligand for the three PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: We support this hypothesis by showing that phosphorylation by at least two protein kinases on several sites in the regulatory region of synGAP-α1 reduces the affinity of synGAP-α1's PDZ-ligand for the three PDZ domains of PSD-95.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figures 3, 6, and 7.

claim: CaMKII is activated when synaptic plasticity is initiated by activation of NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs).
source: One of these protein kinases is CaMKII, which is activated when synaptic plasticity is initiated by activation of NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of synaptic plasticity.

claim: PLK2 is a constitutively active kinase that is induced by neuronal activity and mediates homeostatic scaling.
source: The other is PLK2, a constitutively active kinase that is induced by neuronal activity and mediates homeostatic scaling (Seeburg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seeburg et al., 2005.

claim: Binding of Ca2+/CaM to synGAP-α1 selectively reduces its affinity for PDZ3 of PSD-95.
source: We further show that binding of Ca2+/CaM to synGAP-α1 selectively reduces its affinity for PDZ3 of PSD-95.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 10A.

claim: Reduction of the total amount of synGAP in heterozygous knockout mice alters the composition of PSDs in the mutant mice.
source: Finally, we show that reduction of the total amount of synGAP in heterozygous knockout mice alters the composition of PSDs in the mutant mice in a way that is most directly explained by reduced competition from synGAP-α1 for binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11.

claim: The PSD is an organized complex of signaling proteins attached to the postsynaptic membrane of excitatory glutamatergic synapses in the central nervous system.
source: The PSD is an organized complex of signaling proteins attached to the postsynaptic membrane of excitatory glutamatergic synapses in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: PSD-95 is the most prominent scaffold protein in the PSD.
source: It comprises a network of scaffold proteins, the most prominent of which is PSD-95, a member of the MAGUK family (Membrane-Associated GUanylate Kinase-like proteins) (Kennedy, 2000; Sheng and Kim, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kennedy, 2000 and Sheng and Kim, 2011.

claim: An average PSD (~360 nm in diameter) is estimated to contain ~300 molecules of PSD-95 with 900 PDZ domains.
source: An average PSD (~360 nm in diameter) is estimated to contain ~300 molecules of PSD-95 with 900 PDZ domains (Chen et al., 2005; Sugiyama et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2005 and Sugiyama et al., 2005.

claim: SynGAP is nearly as abundant in the PSD as PSD-95 itself.
source: SynGAP is nearly as abundant in the PSD as PSD-95 itself (Chen et al., 1998; Cheng et al., 2006; Dosemeci et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 1998, Cheng et al., 2006, and Dosemeci et al., 2007.

claim: SynGAP is expressed as several isoforms with four different C-termini, α1, α2, β, and γ.
source: It is expressed as several isoforms with four different C-termini, α1, α2, β, and γ (Li et al., 2001; McMahon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2001 and McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: The α1-containing isoforms of synGAP are abundantly expressed at synapses and contain the PDZ ligand.
source: The α1-containing isoforms are abundantly expressed at synapses and contain the PDZ ligand.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by the literature.

claim: Assuming that α1 isoforms make up 30–50% of the total synaptic synGAP, synGAP-α1 could occupy 10–15% of the PDZ domains of PSD-95 in an average PSD.
source: Assuming that α1 isoforms make up 30–50% of the total synaptic synGAP, and that one synGAP-α1 molecule can bind to any one of the three PDZ domains in each molecule of PSD-95, synGAP-α1 could occupy 10–15% of the PDZ domains of PSD-95 in an average PSD.
evidence: This is calculated based on the relative abundance of synGAP and PSD-95.

claim: SynGAP-α1 could help to regulate the size and strength of the synapse by limiting the availability of 'slots' that can bind AMPAR complexes.
source: Thus, it could help to regulate the size and strength of the synapse by limiting the availability of 'slots' that can bind AMPAR complexes (Hayashi et al., 2000; Shi et al., 2001; Opazo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2000, Shi et al., 2001, and Opazo et al., 2012.

claim: PDZ domains act as flexible protein interaction points that can be modified to support changes in cytoplasmic organization.
source: It has been proposed that, in general, PDZ domains act as flexible protein interaction points that can be modified to support changes in cytoplasmic organization (Kurakin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kurakin et al., 2007.

claim: Complexes formed by PDZ domain interactions are examples of linked, multiple equilibria, the stable configurations of which are determined by the concentrations of each component and by their affinities for the relevant PDZ domains.
source: Complexes formed by PDZ domain interactions are examples of linked, multiple equilibria, the stable configurations of which are determined by the concentrations of each component and by their affinities for the relevant PDZ domains.
evidence: This is a general principle of biochemical equilibria.

claim: PSD-95 protein complexes exist in dynamic equilibrium permitting continual turnover and potential rearrangement of their composition.
source: Evidence has indicated that PSD-95 protein complexes exist in dynamic equilibrium permitting continual turnover and potential rearrangement of their composition (Sturgill et al., 2009; Schapitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sturgill et al., 2009 and Schapitz et al., 2010.

claim: Reduction of synGAP-α1's affinity after phosphorylation will allow other components to compete more effectively for binding to PDZ domains, causing the composition of the PSD-95 complex to shift to a new equilibrium.
source: Because synGAP-α1 is an abundant protein in the PSD with a relatively high affinity for all three PDZ domains of PSD-95, reduction of its affinity after phosphorylation will allow other components to compete more effectively for binding; thus, the composition of the PSD-95 complex will shift to a new equilibrium.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on principles of chemical equilibria.

claim: Phosphorylation by CaMKII in living neurons triggers movement of synGAP away from the PSD.
source: For example, two other groups used imaging to show that phosphorylation by CaMKII in living neurons triggers movement of synGAP away from the PSD (Yang et al., 2013; Araki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2013 and Araki et al., 2015.

claim: Activation of NMDARs and CaMKII causes dispersal of synGAP away from the PSD within a few minutes.
source: Activation of NMDARs and CaMKII causes dispersal of synGAP away from the PSD within a few minutes (Yang et al., 2013; Araki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2013 and Araki et al., 2015.

claim: Activation of NMDARs and CaMKII produces an equally rapid increase in the rate of trapping of AMPARs at synaptic sites.
source: The same stimuli produce an equally rapid increase in the rate of trapping of AMPARs at synaptic sites (Makino and Malinow, 2009; Opazo et al., 2010; Opazo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Makino and Malinow, 2009, Opazo et al., 2010, and Opazo et al., 2012.

claim: The rates of synGAP dispersal and AMPAR trapping are compatible with the notion that reduced binding of synGAP to PSD-95 during induction of LTP opens up binding slots for AMPAR complexes.
source: Thus, the rates of these two processes, observed in living neurons, are compatible with the notion that reduced binding of synGAP to PSD-95 during induction of LTP opens up binding slots for AMPAR complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation of the two processes.

claim: Dispersal of synGAP away from the postsynaptic membrane would be expected to result in increased activation of Ras and Rap.
source: Dispersal of synGAP away from the postsynaptic membrane would be expected to result in increased activation of Ras and Rap, which would lead to increases in the rates of exocytosis and/or endocytosis of AMPARs, respectively (Zhu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on synGAP's GAP activity and is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2002.

claim: Increased exocytosis of AMPARs does not contribute to their increased trapping in the minutes following synaptic stimulation.
source: However, experiments show that increased exocytosis of AMPARs does not contribute to their increased trapping in the minutes following synaptic stimulation (Makino and Malinow, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Makino and Malinow, 2009.

claim: Exocytosis replenishes surface AMPARs in the dendrite and perisynaptic spine membrane with a slower time course than enhanced trapping.
source: Instead, exocytosis replenishes surface AMPARs in the dendrite and perisynaptic spine membrane, and this process occurs with a slower time course than enhanced trapping.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the literature.

claim: Absence of synGAP in hippocampal neurons cultured from synGAP KO fetuses leads to accelerated ('precocious') maturation of spines.
source: An additional example of a previous result that is explained by this model, is the observation that absence of synGAP in hippocampal neurons cultured from synGAP KO fetuses leads to accelerated ('precocious') maturation of spines, including early movement of PSD-95 into spine heads, and ultimately larger clusters of PSD-95 in individual synapses compared to wt neurons (Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Expression of wt-synGAP-α1 in synGAP KO neurons rescued all phenotypes of precocious spine maturation.
source: In this study, expression of wt-synGAP-α1 in the mutant neurons rescued all of these phenotypes
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Expression of synGAP-α1 with a deletion of the five residue PDZ ligand (ΔSXV) failed to rescue any of the effects of synGAP deficiency on precocious maturation of spines.
source: however, expression of synGAP-α1 with a deletion of the five residue PDZ ligand (ΔSXV) failed to rescue any of the effects of synGAP deficiency on precocious maturation of spines.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Expression of synGAPΔSXV caused an increase in the size of clusters of PSD-95 in spines compared to wt neurons.
source: In fact, expression of synGAPΔSXV caused an increase in the size of clusters of PSD-95 in spines compared to wt neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: The failure of synGAPΔSXV to rescue phenotypes was not a result of mislocalization of synGAP-α1.
source: This failure to rescue the phenotypes was not a result of mislocalization of synGAP-α1; synGAPΔSXV localized like wt-synGAP-α1 to developing spine heads.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: The α1 and α2 isoforms of synGAP have markedly different effects on synaptic strength when expressed in primary cultures of forebrain neurons.
source: Yet another result supporting the model is the finding of McMahon et al. (2012) that the α1 and α2 isoforms have markedly different effects on synaptic strength when expressed in primary cultures of forebrain neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: 12 to 36 hr after transfection of neurons with the A1α1 isoform of synGAP, 73% of the neurons were 'silent', compared with 11% of control neurons.
source: For example, 12 to 36 hr after transfection of the neurons with the A1α1 isoform of synGAP, 73% of the neurons were 'silent', that is, had no miniature end-plate potentials (mEPSCs), compared with 11% of control neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: Transfection with the A1α2 isoform of synGAP had no effect on the proportion of silent neurons.
source: In contrast, transfection with the A1α2 isoform, which differs from α1 only in its C-terminal 48 residues and lacks a PDZ ligand, had no effect on the proportion of silent neurons, which remained at 11%.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: Both A1α1 and A1α2 isoforms of synGAP localized normally to dendrites and spines.
source: Like Vazquez et al., (2004), they found that the differential effect did not arise from mislocalization of the A1α2 isoform. Both isoforms of synGAP localized normally to dendrites and spines.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: Neurons cultured from synGAP deficient mice have a higher average number of AMPARs at their synapses than wt neurons.
source: Neurons cultured from synGAP deficient mice have been reported by several groups to have a higher average number of AMPARs at their synapses than wt neurons (Kim et al., 2003; Vazquez et al., 2004; Rumbaugh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2003, Vazquez et al., 2004, and Rumbaugh et al., 2006.

claim: Mutations in a single copy of synGAP have been causally implicated in sporadic cases of non-syndromic ID, often associated with either autism (ASD) or epilepsy.
source: Mutations in a single copy of synGAP have been causally implicated in sporadic cases of non-syndromic ID, often associated with either autism (ASD) or epilepsy (Berryer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berryer et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations causing SynGAP haploinsufficiency appear to account for 2–9% of sporadic cases of developmental ID.
source: Although data is still sparse, mutations causing SynGAP haploinsufficiency appear to account for 2–9% of sporadic cases (Hamdan et al., 2011; Berryer et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hamdan et al., 2011 and Berryer et al., 2013.

claim: The prevalence of SynGAP haploinsufficiency in the population could be as high as 0.03–0.1%.
source: suggesting that its prevalence in the population could be as high as 0.03–0.1% and placing it in the same range of frequency as Fragile-X syndrome.
evidence: This is calculated based on the frequency of sporadic ID and the proportion caused by SynGAP mutations.

claim: The amount of synGAP in the brains of mice with synGAP haploinsufficiency is reduced by 50%.
source: The amount of synGAP in the brains of mice with synGAP haploinsufficiency is reduced by 50% (Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Phosphorylation of r-synGAP-α1 by CaMKII reduces its binding to all of the individual PDZ domains and to PDZ12 and PDZ123.
source: Phosphorylation by CaMKII reduces binding of r-synGAP-α1 to all of the individual PDZ domains and to PDZ12 and PDZ123 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3A.

claim: The reduction in binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains requires the presence of both Ca2+/CaM and CaMKII in the phosphorylation reaction mixture.
source: The reduction in binding requires the presence of both Ca2+/CaM and CaMKII in the phosphorylation reaction mixture (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B.

claim: The reduction in binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains is not caused by phosphorylation of PDZ domains on the column by residual CaMKII.
source: The fourth bar of Figure 3B shows that the reduction in binding is not caused by phosphorylation of PDZ domains on the column by residual CaMKII.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B.

claim: As many as 10 sites on r-synGAP-α1 are phosphorylated by CaMKII.
source: We have shown previously that as many as 10 sites on r-synGAP-α1 are phosphorylated by CaMKII (Walkup et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walkup et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 5 sites on r-synGAP-α1, including site S1123, are fully phosphorylated after a 0.5 min reaction with CaMKII.
source: Approximately 5 of these, including site S1123, are fully phosphorylated after an 0.5 min reaction (Walkup et al., 2015 and Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walkup et al., 2015 and demonstrated in Figure 3C.

claim: The reduction in binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123 is maximal after 0.5 min of phosphorylation by CaMKII.
source: The reduction in binding is maximal after 0.5 min, indicating that phosphorylation of the more rapidly phosphorylated sites is sufficient for full reduction of affinity.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3D.

claim: Phosphorylation of r-synGAP-α1 by CDK5 had no significant effect on its affinity for PDZ123.
source: Phosphorylation by CDK5 had no significant effect on affinity
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3E.

claim: Phosphorylation of r-synGAP-α1 by PLK2 decreased its affinity for PDZ123 by ~40%.
source: whereas, phosphorylation by PLK2 decreased its affinity by ~40%, less strongly than does phosphorylation by CaMKII (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3E.

claim: Both CaMKII and PLK2 can phosphorylate several sites in a region marked MPD (multiple-phosphorylation domain) in Figure 2A, including serines at 808, 810, 821, 825, and 827.
source: Both CaMKII and PLK2 can phosphorylate several sites in a region marked MPD (multiple-phosphorylation domain) in Figure 2A, including serines at 808, 810, 821, 825, and 827 (Walkup et al., 2015; Walkup et al., in preperation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walkup et al., 2015 and Walkup et al., in preparation, and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Phosphorylation of multiple sites at various locations in the regulatory region can decrease binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains, but to varying degrees.
source: This result means that phosphorylation of multiple sites at various locations in the regulatory region can decrease binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains, but to varying degrees.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results with different kinases.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ1 is 220 ± 30 nM.
source: A KD of 220 ± 30 nM (Table 1) was calculated as described under Materials and methods (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is measured experimentally by SPR as shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ2 is 1500 ± 100 nM.
source: Table 1
evidence: This is measured experimentally by SPR as shown in Figure 5A and Table 1.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ3 is 620 ± 70 nM.
source: Table 1
evidence: This is measured experimentally by SPR as shown in Figure 5B and Table 1.

claim: The KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ12 is 350 ± 40 nM.
source: Table 1
evidence: This is measured experimentally by SPR as shown in Figure 5C and Table 1.

claim: The KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ123 is 4.7 ± 0.6 nM.
source: Table 1
evidence: This is measured experimentally by SPR as shown in Figure 5D and Table 1.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, PDZ1 has a higher affinity for r-synGAP-α1 than does PDZ3.
source: These data show that, under these conditions, PDZ1 has a higher affinity for r-synGAP-α1 than does PDZ3.
evidence: This is based on the measured KD values in Table 1.

claim: Single or multiple mutations of serines to alanine (except those including S1283D) did not significantly alter binding of unphosphorylated r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123.
source: Single or multiple mutations of the indicated serines to alanine did not significantly alter binding before phosphorylation; nor did the double mutation S1093D/S1123D.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: Mutations in which site S1283 was mutated to the phosphomimetic aspartate (S1283D and S1093D/S1123D/S1283D) decreased binding of unphosphorylated r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123 with p<0.0001.
source: Only mutations in which site S1283 was mutated to the phosphomimetic aspartate (S1283D and S1093D/S1123D/S1283D) decreased binding of unphosphorylated r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123 with a significant p-value (p<0.0001 for both).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: Phosphorylation of S1283 has the most potent effect of all the sites on binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains.
source: This result suggests that phosphorylation of S1283 has the most potent effect of all the sites on binding to PDZ domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational analysis in Figure 6.

claim: The triple mutant S1093A/S1123A/S1283A was the only S to A mutation that significantly interfered with the loss of binding compared to wild type after 0.5 min of phosphorylation (p=0.0074).
source: In contrast, the triple mutant S1093A/S1123A/S1283A was the only S to A mutation that significantly interfered with the loss of binding (p=0.0074) compared to wild type after 0.5 min of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: Sites S1123 and S1283 both contribute to reduction of binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains after brief phosphorylation.
source: This result reinforces the conclusion that sites S1123 and S1283 both contribute to reduction of binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains after brief phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational analysis in Figure 6.

claim: None of the mutations interfere with the loss of binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains after ten min of phosphorylation.
source: Notably, none of the mutations interfere with the loss of binding to PDZ domains after ten min of phosphorylation (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: Maximum loss of binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains can be accomplished by cumulative phosphorylation over ten min of several sites within the regulatory domain.
source: Taken together, these results and the results of phosphorylation by PLK2 mean that phosphorylation of S1283 and S1123 significantly reduces binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains, however maximum loss of binding can also be accomplished by cumulative phosphorylation over ten min of several sites within the regulatory domain (Figure 2A and Walkup et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results in Figures 3, 6, and 2A.

claim: Phosphorylation for 10 min by CaMKII increases the KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ123 approximately ten-fold.
source: Phosphorylation for 10 min by CaMKII increases the KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 approximately ten-fold (Figure 7A, Table 1)
evidence: This is measured experimentally by SPR as shown in Figure 7A and Table 1.

claim: Mutation of S1283 to aspartate increases the KDapp of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ123 approximately four-fold.
source: whereas mutation of S1283 to aspartate increases the KDapp approximately four-fold (Figure 7B, Table 1).
evidence: This is measured experimentally by SPR as shown in Figure 7B and Table 1.

claim: Cumulative phosphorylation of several residues can reduce affinity of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ domains by an order of magnitude.
source: Thus, cumulative phosphorylation of several residues can reduce affinity for PDZ domains by an order of magnitude
evidence: This is an inference based on the SPR measurements in Figure 7A and Table 1.

claim: Addition of a negative charge at S1283 alone can reduce the affinity of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ domains by a factor of four.
source: whereas, addition of a negative charge at S1283 alone can reduce the affinity by a factor of four.
evidence: This is an inference based on the SPR measurements in Figure 7B and Table 1.

claim: The presence of Ca2+/CaM in reactions with either CDK5/p35 or CDK5/p25 doubled the rate and stoichiometry of phosphorylation of r-synGAP-α1.
source: While studying phosphorylation of r-synGAP-α1 by CDK5 (Walkup et al., 2015), we found that the presence of Ca2+/CaM in reactions with either CDK5/p35 or CDK5/p25 doubled the rate and stoichiometry of the phosphorylation (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Inclusion of Ca2+ or CaM alone in the phosphorylation reactions did not alter the rates or stoichiometry of r-synGAP-α1 phosphorylation by CDK5.
source: Inclusion of Ca2+ or CaM alone in the phosphorylation reactions did not alter the rates or stoichiometry.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Ca2+/CaM binds directly to r-synGAP-α1, causing a substrate-directed enhancement of its phosphorylation by CDK5.
source: This result suggests that Ca2+/CaM binds directly to r-synGAP-α1, causing a substrate-directed enhancement of its phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effect of Ca2+/CaM on phosphorylation of r-synGAP-α1 versus histone H1.

claim: R-synGAP-α1 binds to a CaM-Sepharose affinity resin in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: To further verify that Ca2+/CaM binds directly to r-synGAP-α1, we showed that r-synGAP-α1 binds to a CaM-Sepharose affinity resin in a Ca2+-dependent manner, as would be expected if it binds Ca2+/CaM specifically and with significant affinity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of Ca2+/CaM alone in a Ras- or Rap-GAP assay has no effect on the GAP activity of r-synGAP-α1.
source: We found that the presence of Ca2+/CaM alone in a Ras- or Rap-GAP assay has no effect on the GAP activity of r-synGAP-α1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for Ca2+/CaM is 9 ± 1 nM as measured by SPR.
source: Analysis of the equilibrium phase of association at each concentration (Figure 9B) yielded a KD of 9 ± 1 nM, indicative of high affinity binding.
evidence: This is measured experimentally by SPR as shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: The KD of r-synGAP-α1 for Ca2+/CaM is 31 ± 3 nM as measured by CaM-Sepharose binding assay.
source: The data were fit to hyperbolic curves and the KD's for binding of r-synGAP-α1 and sr-synGAP to Ca2+/CaM were calculated to be 31 ± 3 nM and 210 ± 30 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is measured experimentally by CaM-Sepharose binding as shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The KD of sr-synGAP for Ca2+/CaM is 210 ± 30 nM as measured by CaM-Sepharose binding assay.
source: The data were fit to hyperbolic curves and the KD's for binding of r-synGAP-α1 and sr-synGAP to Ca2+/CaM were calculated to be 31 ± 3 nM and 210 ± 30 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is measured experimentally by CaM-Sepharose binding as shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The high affinity Ca2+/CaM binding site appears to be located in the regulatory disordered region of r-synGAP-α1, which is missing in sr-synGAP.
source: Thus, the high affinity site appears to be located in the regulatory disordered region of r-synGAP-α1, which is missing in sr-synGAP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in affinity between r-synGAP-α1 and sr-synGAP.

claim: Binding of Ca2+/CaM has a more specific, but weaker, effect on binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ domains than does phosphorylation.
source: Thus, binding of Ca2+/CaM has a more specific, but weaker, effect on binding to the PDZ domains than does phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of results in Figures 3A and 10A.

claim: The effects of phosphorylation and of the presence of Ca2+/CaM during incubation with resin are not additive on binding of r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123.
source: The effects of phosphorylation and of the presence of Ca2+/CaM during incubation with resin are not additive (Figure 10B)
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 10B.

claim: The presence of Ca2+/CaM during the incubation with resin does not further decrease binding of phosphorylated r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123.
source: that is, the presence of Ca2+/CaM during the incubation with resin does not further decrease binding of phosphorylated r-synGAP-α1 to PDZ123.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 10B.

claim: In molar terms, synGAP-α1 is 30–50% as abundant in the PSD as PSD-95 itself.
source: In molar terms, synGAP-α1 is 30–50% as abundant in the PSD as PSD-95 itself (Chen et al., 1998; Cheng et al., 2006; Dosemeci et al., 2007; Sheng and Hoogenraad, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 1998, Cheng et al., 2006, Dosemeci et al., 2007, and Sheng and Hoogenraad, 2007.

claim: Syngap+/- mice have about half as much synGAP in homogenates from forebrain as wt littermates.
source: Syngap+/- mice have been shown to have about half as much synGAP in homogenates from forebrain as wt littermates.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: The level of synGAP is decreased in relation to PSD-95 by ~ 24% in PSDs from the Syngap+/- mice (p=0.0007, d = 1.75).
source: As predicted, the level of synGAP is decreased in relation to PSD-95 by ~ 24% in PSDs (p=0.0007, d = 1.75) from the Syngap+/- mice (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11A.

claim: The ratios of TARPs 2,3,4,ɣ8 to PSD-95 are significantly increased (~12%, p=0.017, d = 0.93) in PSDs from Syngap+/- mice.
source: Furthermore, the ratios of TARPs 2,3,4,ɣ8, and of LRRTM2 to PSD-95 are significantly increased (Figure 11B,C; TARP/PSD-95, ~12%, p=0.017, d = 0.93
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11B.

claim: The ratio of LRRTM2 to PSD-95 is significantly increased (~14%, p=0.0035, d = 0.66) in PSDs from Syngap+/- mice.
source: Furthermore, the ratios of TARPs 2,3,4,ɣ8, and of LRRTM2 to PSD-95 are significantly increased (Figure 11B,C; TARP/PSD-95, ~12%, p=0.017, d = 0.93; LRRTM2/PSD-95, ~14%, p=0.0035, d = 0.66).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11C.

claim: The ratio of neuroligin-1 to PSD-95 is unchanged in the Syngap+/- mice (d = 0.07).
source: Interestingly, the ratio of neuroligin-1 to PSD-95 is unchanged in the Syngap+/- mice (d = 0.07, Figure 11D)
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11D.

claim: The ratio of neuroligin-2 to PSD-95 is increased by ~9% (p=0.019, d = 0.64) in PSDs from Syngap+/- mice.
source: However, the ratio of neuroligin-2 to PSD-95 (Figure 11E) is increased by ~9% (p=0.019, d = 0.64).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 11E.

claim: Neuroligin-2 normally associates mostly with inhibitory synapses and mediates their maturation.
source: Neuroligin-2 normally associates mostly with inhibitory synapses and mediates their maturation (Varoqueaux et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Varoqueaux et al., 2004.

claim: Over-expression of PSD-95 in neurons causes a redistribution of neuroligin-2, increasing the proportion associated with excitatory synapses.
source: However, Levinson et al. (2005) reported that over-expression of PSD-95 in neurons causes a redistribution of neuroligin-2, increasing the proportion associated with excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levinson et al., 2005.

claim: The effect of reduction of synGAP on the distribution of neuroligin-2 is the same as the effect of over-expression of PSD-95.
source: Thus, the effect of reduction of synGAP on the distribution of neuroligin-2 shown here is the same as the effect of over-expression of PSD-95, suggesting that both manipulations increase the number of PDZ3 domains available for binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the current results with those of Levinson et al., 2005.

claim: A decrease in availability of synGAP in the PSD scaffold increases the association of TARPs, LRRTMs, and neuroligin-2 with the PSD in vivo by releasing a restriction on binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: Taken together, these results verify the prediction that a decrease in availability of synGAP in the PSD scaffold, increases the association of TARPs, LRRTMs, and neuroligin-2 with the PSD in vivo by releasing a restriction on binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results in Figure 11.

claim: Phosphorylation of synGAP results in 'dispersion' of synGAP away from the PSD and has the effect of upregulating Ras near the PSD.
source: In the Araki study, the authors suggested that phosphorylation of synGAP results in 'dispersion' of synGAP away from the PSD and therefore has the effect of upregulating Ras near the PSD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Araki et al., 2015.

claim: An additional important consequence of the decrease in binding of synGAP to the PDZ domains of PSD-95 is readjustment of the composition of the PSD resulting from increased availability of the PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: We propose here that an additional important consequence of the decrease in binding of synGAP to the PDZ domains of PSD-95 is readjustment of the composition of the PSD resulting from increased availability of the PDZ domains of PSD-95.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental results.

claim: The dynamics of movements of synGAP and AMPARs visualized in living neurons following synaptic stimulation are consistent with the hypothesis that reduced binding of synGAP to PSD-95 opens up binding slots for AMPAR complexes.
source: Indeed, the dynamics of movements of synGAP and AMPARs visualized in living neurons following synaptic stimulation are consistent with this hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation of synGAP dispersal and AMPAR trapping.

claim: The rates of synGAP dispersal and AMPAR trapping are compatible with the notion that reduced binding of synGAP to PSD-95 during induction of LTP opens up binding slots for AMPAR complexes.
source: Thus, the rates of these two processes, observed in living neurons, are compatible with the notion that reduced binding of synGAP to PSD-95 during induction of LTP opens up binding slots for AMPAR complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation of the two processes.

claim: Absence of synGAP in hippocampal neurons cultured from synGAP KO fetuses leads to early movement of PSD-95 into spine heads.
source: An additional example of a previous result that is explained by this model, is the observation that absence of synGAP in hippocampal neurons cultured from synGAP KO fetuses leads to accelerated ('precocious') maturation of spines, including early movement of PSD-95 into spine heads, and ultimately larger clusters of PSD-95 in individual synapses compared to wt neurons (Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Absence of synGAP in hippocampal neurons cultured from synGAP KO fetuses leads to ultimately larger clusters of PSD-95 in individual synapses compared to wt neurons.
source: An additional example of a previous result that is explained by this model, is the observation that absence of synGAP in hippocampal neurons cultured from synGAP KO fetuses leads to accelerated ('precocious') maturation of spines, including early movement of PSD-95 into spine heads, and ultimately larger clusters of PSD-95 in individual synapses compared to wt neurons (Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: SynGAPΔSXV localized like wt-synGAP-α1 to developing spine heads.
source: This failure to rescue the phenotypes was not a result of mislocalization of synGAP-α1; synGAPΔSXV localized like wt-synGAP-α1 to developing spine heads.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: The data are consistent with the idea that synGAP-α1 normally competes with several proteins for binding to the PDZ domains of PSD-95, and thus limits the size of clusters of PSD-95 and its associated proteins, as well as their movement into spine heads.
source: Instead, the data are consistent with the idea that synGAP-α1 normally competes with several proteins for binding to the PDZ domains of PSD-95, and thus limits the size of clusters of PSD-95 and its associated proteins, as well as their movement into spine heads (Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the results from Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: The A1α2 isoform of synGAP differs from α1 only in its C-terminal 48 residues and lacks a PDZ ligand.
source: In contrast, transfection with the A1α2 isoform, which differs from α1 only in its C-terminal 48 residues and lacks a PDZ ligand, had no effect on the proportion of silent neurons, which remained at 11%.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: The differential effect of A1α1 and A1α2 isoforms on silent neurons did not arise from mislocalization of the A1α2 isoform.
source: Like Vazquez et al., (2004), they found that the differential effect did not arise from mislocalization of the A1α2 isoform.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: The most straightforward explanation of the differential effect of A1α1 and A1α2 isoforms is that overexpression of the synGAP-α1 isoform bearing the PDZ ligand restricts binding of AMPAR auxiliary proteins to PDZ domains and thus interferes with their localization to the synaptic site.
source: The most straightforward explanation of this result is consistent with our hypothesis, which predicts that overexpression of the synGAP-α1 isoform bearing the PDZ ligand restricts binding of AMPAR auxiliary proteins to PDZ domains and thus interfers with their localization to the synaptic site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' hypothesis and the results from McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: The increase in AMPARs in Syngap+/- mice may be a direct result of increased binding of TARPs and LRRTMs to PDZ domains that are made available by the reduced amount of synGAP.
source: The data presented here suggests that the increase in AMPARs in Syngap+/- mice may be a direct result of increased binding of TARPs and LRRTMs to PDZ domains that are made available by the reduced amount of synGAP (Tomita et al., 2005; de Wit et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' experimental results and is supported by citations to Tomita et al., 2005 and de Wit et al., 2009.

claim: Mutations causing SynGAP haploinsufficiency appear to account for 2–9% of sporadic cases of developmental ID.
source: Although data is still sparse, mutations causing SynGAP haploinsufficiency appear to account for 2–9% of sporadic cases (Hamdan et al., 2011; Berryer et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hamdan et al., 2011 and Berryer et al., 2013.

claim: The prevalence of SynGAP haploinsufficiency in the population could be as high as 0.03–0.1%, placing it in the same range of frequency as Fragile-X syndrome.
source: suggesting that its prevalence in the population could be as high as 0.03–0.1% and placing it in the same range of frequency as Fragile-X syndrome.
evidence: This is calculated based on the frequency of sporadic ID and the proportion caused by SynGAP mutations.

claim: The reduction in synGAP in Syngap+/- mice leads to a shift in the composition of the PSD scaffold, apparently resulting from the decrease in synGAP's ability to compete for binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: We show here that this reduction leads to a shift in the composition of the PSD scaffold, apparently resulting from the decrease in synGAP's ability to compete for binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results in Figure 11.

claim: The derangement in PSD composition caused by synGAP haploinsufficiency is likely a significant factor in the human pathology leading to ID, ASD, and epilepsy.
source: This derangement is likely a significant factor in the human pathology leading to ID, ASD, and epilepsy.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the authors' experimental results and the known association of SYNGAP1 mutations with these disorders.

claim: SynGAP begins to be expressed at birth in the mouse brain and its expression increases rapidly as synapses are forming during the first weeks after birth.
source: In the mouse brain, synGAP begins to be expressed at birth and its expression increases rapidly as synapses are forming during the first weeks after birth (Vazquez et al., 2004; Barnett et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and Barnett et al., 2006.

claim: Newborns with complete deletion of Syngap appear normal, but die a few days after birth with movement defects and apparent seizure activity.
source: Newborns with complete deletion of Syngap appear normal, but die a few days after birth with movement defects and apparent seizure activity, indicating a defect as synapses are forming (Kim et al., 2003; Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2003 and Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Syngap heterozygous mice appear normal and survive into adulthood with no apparent alterations in gross brain morphology, but with defects in behavior and synaptic plasticity.
source: Syngap heterozygous mice also appear normal and survive into adulthood with no apparent alterations in gross brain morphology, but with defects in behavior and synaptic plasticity (Komiyama et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Komiyama et al., 2002.

claim: Syngap+/- neurons have, on average, larger spine heads than wt neurons.
source: and, have, on average, larger spine heads (Vazquez et al., 2004; Carlisle et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and Carlisle et al., 2008.

claim: Syngap+/- neurons form excitatory synapses precociously in culture.
source: They form excitatory synapses precociously in culture (Vazquez et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Syngap+/- neurons form excitatory synapses precociously during postnatal cortical and hippocampal development.
source: and also during postnatal cortical and hippocampal development (Clement et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clement et al., 2012.

claim: Precocious synapse formation in Syngap+/- neurons leads to an elevated E/I ratio (excitatory/inhibitory synaptic ratio) and derangement of critical developmental periods.
source: leading to an elevated E/I ratio (excitatory/inhibitory synaptic ratio) and derangement of critical developmental periods (Clement et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clement et al., 2013.

claim: The increased presence of TARPs, LRRTMs, and neuroligin-2 in PSDs of young Syngap+/- animals is likely a primary, rather than a secondary effect of the mutation.
source: While all of these influences could contribute to alterations in the composition of PSDs in Syngap+/- animals, several arguments suggest that the increased presence of TARPs, LRRTMs, and neuroligin-2 that we report in PSDs of young animals (Figure 11) is likely a primary, rather than a secondary effect of the mutation.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of overexpression of synGAP-α1 in cultured forebrain neurons on development of spines is rapid, measurable within 12–24 hr of transfection.
source: The effect of overexpression of synGAP-α1 in cultured forebrain neurons on development of spines (Vazquez et al., 2004) and on numbers of synaptic AMPARs (McMahon et al., 2012) is rapid, measurable within 12–24 hr of transfection
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: The effect of overexpression of synGAP-α1 on spine development and AMPAR numbers is not caused by mislocalization of the exogenous synGAP-α1.
source: and is not caused by mislocalization of the exogenous synGAP- α1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: The effects of overexpression of synGAP-α1 on spine development and AMPAR numbers are not dependent on the GAP activity of synGAP and they require the PDZ ligand.
source: They are also not dependent on the GAP activity of synGAP and they require the PDZ ligand.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vazquez et al., 2004 and McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: The hypothesis that synGAP-α1 restricts binding to PDZ domains is the most parsimonious explanation for the specific effects of synGAP-α1 on PSD composition.
source: Thus, the hypothesis we have put forward is the most parsimonious explanation for the specific effects of synGAP-α1 on PSD composition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the authors' analysis of the evidence.

claim: The change in protein composition of PSDs in Syngap+/- animals cannot be explained by a two-fold reduction in RasGAP and RapGAP activity.
source: Similarly, the change in protein composition of PSDs in Syngap+/- animals (Figure 11) cannot be explained by a two-fold reduction in RasGAP and RapGAP activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known activities of synGAP and the expected consequences of reduced GAP activity.

claim: SynGAP produces a much larger fold increase in GTPase activity of Rap than of Ras.
source: SynGAP produces a much larger fold increase in GTPase activity of Rap than of Ras (Walkup et al., 2015 and references therein).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walkup et al., 2015 and references therein.

claim: Loss of half of the GAP activity would be predicted to increase the level of active Rap even more than that of active Ras.
source: Therefore, loss of half of the GAP activity would be predicted to increase the level of active Rap even more than that of active Ras.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative GAP activities of synGAP toward Rap and Ras.

claim: An increase in active Rap relative to active Ras would be expected to result in a relative increase in endocytosis of AMPARs compared to exocytosis.
source: Thus, one would expect a relative increase in endocytosis of AMPARs compared to exocytosis (Zhu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known roles of Ras and Rap in AMPAR trafficking and is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2002.

claim: A relative increase in endocytosis of AMPARs would result in fewer AMPAR binding proteins in the PSD, not more as observed in Syngap+/- mice.
source: That would result in fewer AMPAR binding proteins in the PSD; not more, as we observe.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expected consequences of increased AMPAR endocytosis.

claim: Application of Occam's razor strongly favors the hypothesis that synGAP-α1 restricts binding to PDZ domains.
source: For now, application of Occam's razor strongly favors the hypothesis we have presented.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the authors' analysis of the evidence.

claim: Future experiments will be necessary to determine the quantitative significance of synGAP-α1's restriction of PDZ domain binding sites at various times during development and during acute stimulation of synapses.
source: Future experiments will be necessary to determine the quantitative significance of synGAP-α1's restriction of PDZ domain binding sites at various times during development and during acute stimulation of synapses.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Acute phosphorylation of synGAP-α1 by CaMKII following activation of NMDARs during induction of LTP could initiate rearrangement of the composition of PSDs of individual synapses.
source: Thus, acute phosphorylation of synGAP-α1 by CaMKII following activation of NMDARs during induction of LTP could initiate rearrangement of the composition of PSDs of individual synapses by causing an increase in equilibrium binding in the PSD of AMPARs associated with TARPs and LRRTMs, and of other PSD-95 binding proteins, as they diffuse from perisynaptic locations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the authors' experimental results and the known dynamics of LTP.

claim: It will be important to test the prediction that acute phosphorylation of synGAP-α1 initiates rearrangement of PSD composition in future experiments.
source: It will be important to test this prediction in future experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Dephosphorylation of synGAP-α1 after its movement away from PDZ domains might be expected to allow synGAP-α1 to displace the newly added TARPs and LRRTMs and reverse the addition of new AMPARs.
source: Dephosphorylation of synGAP-α1 after its movement away from PDZ domains might be expected to allow synGAP-α1 to displace the newly added TARPs and LRRTMs and reverse the addition of new AMPARs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the reversibility of phosphorylation.

claim: Additional processes occurring later in the consolidation of LTP would be needed to stabilize the newly added AMPARs in the synapse and/or to permanently decrease the number of synGAP-α1 molecules per PSD-95 in potentiated synapses.
source: Thus, if this model is correct, additional processes occurring later in the consolidation of LTP would be needed to stabilize the newly added AMPARs in the synapse and/or to permanently decrease the number of synGAP-α1 molcules per PSD-95 in potentiated synapses.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the need for stable changes during LTP consolidation.

claim: Such processes could include degradation of the phosphorylated synGAP-α1 and its replacement by newly synthesized alternatively-spliced isoforms that lack the C-terminal PDZ binding domain.
source: Such processes could include degradation of the phosphorylated synGAP-α1 and its replacement by newly synthesized alternatively-spliced isoforms that lack the C-terminal PDZ binding domain (Li et al., 2001; McMahon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Li et al., 2001 and McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: An increase in localization of neuroligin-2 at excitatory synapses is mediated by binding to PSD-95 and increases the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory synaptic contacts.
source: Several studies have shown that an increase in localization of neuroligin-2 at excitatory synapses is mediated by binding to PSD-95 and increases the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory synaptic contacts (Prange et al., 2004; Levinson et al., 2005; 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prange et al., 2004, Levinson et al., 2005, and Levinson et al., 2010.

claim: The restriction by synGAP-α1 of binding of neuroligin-2 to PDZ3 of PSD-95 would be more significant during development, during formation of new synapses, or perhaps in later phases of consolidation of LTP in adults.
source: It seems likely that the restriction by synGAP-α1 of binding of neuroligin-2 to PDZ3 of PSD-95 would be more significant during development, during formation of new synapses, or perhaps in later phases of consolidation of LTP in adults.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known roles of neuroligin-2 in synapse development.

claim: It is not clear whether a pool of perisynaptic neuroligin-2 exists at adult synapses that could be recruited to new synaptic sites over a few minutes after phosphorylation of synGAP-α1.
source: It is not clear whether a pool of perisynaptic neuroligin-2 exists at adult synapses that could be recruited to new synaptic sites over a few minutes after phosphorylation of synGAP-α1.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the localization of neuroligin-2.

claim: The small but significant increase in neuroligin-2 in excitatory PSDs from Syngap+/- mice, as well as the increased steady state amounts of TARPs and LRRTMs would increase the overall excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance of synapses onto neurons in the mutant mice.
source: Nonetheless, the small but significant increase in neuroligin-2 that we observe in excitatory PSDs from Syngap+/- mice, as well as the increased steady state amounts of TARPs and LRRTMs would increase the overall excitatory/inihibitory (E/I) balance of synapses onto neurons in the mutant mice, and perhaps also in humans with SYNGAP1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results in Figure 11 and the known roles of these proteins.

claim: The increased E/I balance in Syngap+/- mice might also occur in humans with SYNGAP1 haploinsufficiency.
source: Nonetheless, the small but significant increase in neuroligin-2 that we observe in excitatory PSDs from Syngap+/- mice, as well as the increased steady state amounts of TARPs and LRRTMs would increase the overall excitatory/inihibitory (E/I) balance of synapses onto neurons in the mutant mice, and perhaps also in humans with SYNGAP1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the similarity between mouse and human synGAP haploinsufficiency.

claim: The reduction in affinity of synGAP-α1 for PDZ domains of PSD-95 after phosphorylation by CaMKII is apparently not sufficient for complete dispersal of synGAP-α1 away from the PSD.
source: We note that the reduction in affinity of synGAP-α1 for PDZ domains of PSD-95 after phosphorylation by CaMKII is apparently not sufficient for complete dispersal of synGAP-α1 away from the PSD, although it is likely necessary.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and the literature.

claim: Mutated synGAP-α1 missing the PDZ ligand (synGAPΔSXV) cannot bind to PDZ domains, yet still localizes to synaptic spines.
source: Mutated synGAP-α1 missing the PDZ ligand (synGAPΔSXV) cannot bind to PDZ domains, yet still localizes to synaptic spines (Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazquez et al., 2004.

claim: Both α1 and α2 synGAP isoforms localize to the PSD core.
source: Furthermore, Yang et al. (2013) showed by immunoelectron microscopy that both α1 and α2 synGAP isoforms localize to the PSD core
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2013.

claim: α2 isoforms of synGAP are present in isolated PSDs.
source: and McMahon et al. (2012) showed by mass spectrometry that α2 isoforms are present in isolated PSDs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2012.

claim: Reduction of affinity of synGAP for PDZ domains may be sufficient to decrease its ability to compete for binding slots on PSD-95.
source: These data mean that reduction of affinity of synGAP for PDZ domains may be sufficient to decrease its ability to compete for binding slots on PSD-95
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data from the literature.

claim: Complete detachment of synGAP from the PSD in vivo likely requires additional events beyond reduction of affinity for PDZ domains.
source: however, complete detachment of synGAP from the PSD in vivo likely requires additional events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data from the literature.

claim: Binding of Ca2+/CaM alters the conformation of the carboxyl terminal regulatory domain of r-synGAP-α1 allowing CDK5 to phosphorylate additional sites.
source: We have shown that binding of Ca2+/CaM alters the conformation of the carboxyl terminal regulatory domain of r-synGAP-α1 allowing CDK5 to phosphorylate additional sites
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Binding of Ca2+/CaM reduces the affinity of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ3 by ~25%.
source: the binding also reduces the affinity of r-synGAP-α1 for PDZ3 by ~25%.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 10A.

claim: The high copy number of synGAP in the PSD may provide a clue to the functional significance of Ca2+/CaM binding to synGAP.
